aspects.says: A data race is harmless only when every value a read can see gives the right answer: an idempotent computation, a value read in one access, and one read into a local.
basis: section:A Data Race Is Harmless Only When Every Value the Read Can See Gives the Right Answer

aspects.says: A data race is two accesses to one variable from different threads, at least one a write, with no happens-before order between them; timing is not part of the definition.
basis: section:A Data Race Is Two Accesses to One Variable, One a Write, With No Happens-Before Between Them

aspects.says: jcstress runs actors against fresh state millions of times in several JVM configurations and counts each outcome; its verdict holds per machine.
basis: section:A Passing Stress Test Shows Only the Interleavings That Run Produced
aspects.reason: described, not run: the tool is not in the offline runner, and its verdicts depend on the machine, which a graded test must not

aspects.says: Code whose every access is atomic or volatile has no data race and can still race: a check and an act are two steps another thread can run between.
basis: section:Code With No Data Race Can Still Race: a Check and an Act Are Two Steps

aspects.says: One atomic call (putIfAbsent, remove(key, value), compareAndSet, compute) decides between racing threads; a check followed by a separate act does not.
basis: section:Code With No Data Race Can Still Race: a Check and an Act Are Two Steps

aspects.says: A multithreaded test that passes shows only the interleavings its runs produced; an outcome the JLS allows may never appear on one machine, and a thread dump shows no data race.
basis: section:A Passing Stress Test Shows Only the Interleavings That Run Produced

aspects.says: A check-then-act is tested deterministically by pausing one thread between the check and the act while another runs.
basis: section:A Check-Then-Act Is Tested by Pausing One Thread Between the Check and the Act
aspects.reason: this is how the unit's two code practices grade the reader's code; the reader writes the code under test, not the test, so it is used rather than practised
